spoken: On the 4th of November 1945, Hungarians chose freely among several parties, and the Communists won 17 percent.
On the 15th of May 1949, voters got a single list, and a ballot with no mark on it counted as a yes.
Officially, 95.6 percent of those who voted backed the list.
In between, Hungary lost its freedom slice by slice. This is how, and why it still mattered in October 1956.
Hungary had gone to war on Germany's side, and in March 1944 German troops occupied the country.
That year, about 437,000 Jews were deported from Hungary, most of them to be murdered at Auschwitz.
In the autumn, the Red Army fought its way in, and Budapest was besieged from December until February 1945.
By April, the Germans had been driven out, and an estimated 40 percent of the nation's wealth was destroyed.
The Soviet soldiers who drove them out also looted, and very many women were raped.
Some 600,000 Hungarians, soldiers and civilians, were taken to Soviet camps, and about a third never came home.
The historian Dyurdy Dyar-mah-tee calls it a half liberation, free of the Nazis but occupied.
In January 1945, a provisional government formed in Deb-reh-tsen signed an armistice.
Real power now lay with the Allied Control Commission, chaired by the Soviet marshal Kliment Voroshilov.
In March 1945, a land reform broke up the great estates, and some 640,000 poor peasants received land.
On the 4th of November 1945, six parties approved by the Control Commission stood in a general election.
The ballot was secret, and 92.5 percent of registered voters took part.
The Independent Smallholders' Party won about 57 percent, a majority on its own.
The Social Democrats won 17.4 percent, and the Communists of Mah-chahsh Rah-koshee won 17.
The American representative in Budapest reported no evidence that the election was anything but free.
But the Allies required a coalition, and only 9 of its 18 ministers were Smallholders.
Voroshilov vetoed a Smallholder at the Interior Ministry, which ran the police.
It went to the Communist Im-reh Nodge, the man who would lead the government in 1956.
The political police, run by Gah-bor Pay-ter, answered to the Communists from the start.
In February 1946, Hungary became a republic, with the Smallholder Zol-tahn Til-dee as president.
Meanwhile, money collapsed. By July 1946, prices doubled about every 15 hours, the worst inflation ever recorded.
In August, the forint replaced the worthless peng-gur.
Rah-koshee later called his method salami tactics, cutting rivals away one slice at a time.
In late 1946, the political police announced a conspiracy against the republic, and arrested Smallholder deputies.
Their confessions were forced out of them by torture, at the political police headquarters on On-drah-shee Avenue.
Parliament refused to lift the immunity of the party's secretary general, Bay-lah Koh-vahtch, so Soviet soldiers arrested him on the 25th of February 1947.
He spent eight years in Soviet prisons and camps.
In May, Prime Minister Feh-rents Nodge, accused while on holiday in Switzerland, resigned and stayed abroad.
Before the next election, on the 31st of August 1947, about 467,000 people were struck off the voters' rolls.
On the day, Communist activists drove from station to station, voting again and again with blue slips meant for voters away from home.
The number of false votes is disputed. The police chief counted nearly 63,000, and other estimates go up to about 200,000.
The Communists came first with 22 percent, and the Smallholders fell to 15.
Opposition parties still won about 40 percent between them. Then the Independence Party's 49 seats were annulled.
The Communists called 1948 the year of the turn. On the 25th of March, every factory with more than 100 workers was taken over in a single day.
In June, the Social Democrats were merged into the Communist Party, which became the Hungarian Working People's Party, the MDP.
Social Democrats who refused, like Anna Kayt-lee, were pushed out, and President Til-dee was forced to resign.
On the 15th of May 1949, voters got one list, the People's Front's, drawn up by the MDP.
A yes needed no mark. The ballot went into the box as it was.
A no meant crossing out a circle with two lines, behind a curtain, where taking too long could be noted.
On the 20th of August 1949, a constitution on the Soviet model made Hungary a People's Republic.
A new state emblem with a red star replaced the old Koh-shoot arms, on flags too.
On the 26th of December 1948, police arrested Cardinal Yo-zhef Mind-sen-tee, head of Hungary's Catholics, and he was sentenced to life.
In 1948, Stalin had broken with Tito, Yugoslavia's Communist leader, and every Soviet ally now hunted for Titoists.
Hungary's chosen victim was Lahs-loh Royk, a veteran of the Spanish Civil War and a former interior minister.
He was charged with spying for the West and plotting with Tito, and his trial in September 1949 went out on the radio.
Royk confessed to everything. Every question and every answer had been written in advance.
Witnesses later told the UN that the accused had been tortured, and that Yah-nosh Kah-dahr, the interior minister, had promised Royk his life for a confession.
On the 15th of October 1949, Royk was hanged with Tee-bor Sur-nyee and On-drahsh Saw-law-ee. Secret side trials followed.
Rah-koshee told the party to look behind every mistake for the hand of the enemy.
The lesson was plain. Nobody was safe. In 1951, Kah-dahr himself was arrested, and later sentenced to life on invented charges.
Only in March 1956 did the regime admit that the charges against Royk had been fabricated.
By the early 1950s, power lay with one party, and within it with one man, Mah-chahsh Rah-koshee.
His portrait hung beside Stalin's, and the press called him Stalin's best Hungarian disciple.
For his 60th birthday, on the 9th of March 1952, gifts from all over the country filled a palace in Budapest.
That August, he became prime minister as well.
The five-year plan drove heavy industry, and a new steelworks on the Danube was named after Stalin.
Peasants were driven into collective farms, the AVH watched everyone, and by 1953 real wages were a fifth lower than in 1949.
On the 5th of March 1953, Stalin died. Three days later, Hungary's parliament wrote his immortal memory into law.
In eight years, a free vote had become a single list, and a coalition a dictatorship, guarded by Soviet troops.
Terror, deportations, poverty and foreign troops would bring Hungarians onto the streets in October 1956.
And they would cut the red-star emblem out of their flags. Why they rose is the next story.
